About The Author:
I was born in Holyoke, Massachusetts on April 25, 1976.  At a young age I developed a love of reading, writing, drawing and creating that stayed with me throughout high school and college.  My work as a preschool paraprofessional and children's librarian nurtured this love into a desire to publish my own books for children.  My first picture book Too Much Glue was released by Flashlight Press September 1, 2013.  I have been lucky to visit thousands of students in hundreds of classrooms since that day.  The greatest part of my journey into publication has been connecting with students and teachers and attempting to impart some of my love for being an author onto them.

Too Much Glue has received national recognition.  It was the 2016 Montana Treasure State Award Winner in the primary division. In 2014 it received a Play On Words PAL Award which recognizes outstanding children’s products that engender play, advance language and appeal to all children for lasting value.  It received a 2014 Creative Child Magazine Preferred Choice Award in the Kid’s Books category and was chosen for the 2013 ABC Best Books for Children Catalog.  The book is also recommended nationally by Elmer's Glue and included in the Elmer's World of Glue Free Teaching Guide.  It was on the Alabama Camellia Award list 2014-15, Grade 2-3 Division and was a finalist on the NY State Charlotte Award list, 2015-16.

About The Author:
Kate Messner is passionately curious and writes books that encourage kids to wonder, too. Her titles include award-winning picture books like Over and Under the Rainforest, Up in the Garden and Down in the Dirt, The Next President, and How to Read a Story; novels that tackle real-world issues like Chirp, Breakout, All the Answers, and The Seventh Wish; high-interest nonfiction like Tracking Pythons and the History Smashers series; the Fergus and Zeke easy readers; and the popular Ranger in Time chapter books about a time-traveling search and rescue dog.

Kate’s titles are frequently selected for One School, One Book and One School/One Author programs and other community-wide reads. Her books have been New York Times Notable, Junior Library Guild, IndieBound, and Bank Street College of Education Best Books selections. Her novel The Brilliant Fall of Gianna Z. won the E.B. White Read Aloud Medal, and her science picture books have been finalists for the American Academy for the Advancement of Sciences/Subaru SB&F prize for excellence in science writing. In 2020, Kate was honored with New York’s Knickerbocker Award for creating a superior body of work supporting curriculum and educational goals.

Before becoming a full-time writer, Kate was a TV news reporter as well as a National Board Certified educator. She grew up in Medina, NY and graduated from Syracuse University’s S.I. Newhouse School with a degree in Broadcast Journalism. Kate spent seven years working as a television news producer and reporter in Syracuse, NY and Burlington, VT before going back to school to earn a master’s degree in education for secondary-level English Language Arts. She taught middle school language arts for fifteen years before leaving the classroom to write full time but still spends much of her time in schools, working with kids as a visiting author.

Kate lives on Lake Champlain with her family and is trying to summit all 46 Adirondack High Peaks in between book deadlines. Learn more at her website: www.katemessner.com and follow her on Twitter @katemessner.

Follow April on Instagram and Facebook @thecalendarkids for more information on future books in the Calendar Kids collection! About The Illustrator:
Christopher Silas Neal is an award-winning author and illustrator of picture books including the Over and Under series with author Kate Messner, which was praised for its "stunning retro-style illustrations" (New York Times). He makes books that feature animals, shapes, science, friendship and silliness, and strives to create diverse and inclusive characters that reflect the kids and parents who read his books. Neal's author debut titled "Everyone" was praised by Publisher's Weekly as "simple, honest, lyrical". His board book series (Animals Colors, Animal Shapes) received starred reviews from Publisher's Weekly and Kirkus. He speaks about his books, the art making process, and his career at schools, conferences, libraries and book festivals across the country. Neal is a Mexican/Eurpoean-American artist who lives with his wife and two boys in Brooklyn, NY.

About The Author:
Pat Zietlow Miller knew she wanted to be a writer ever since her seventh-grade English teacher read her paper about square-dancing skirts out loud in class and said: "This is the first time anything a student has written has given me chills." (Thanks, Mrs. Mueller! You rock!)

Pat started out as a newspaper reporter and wrote about everything from dartball and deer-hunting to diets and decoupage. Then, she joined an insurance company and edited its newsletter and magazine.

Now, she writes insurance information by day and children's books by night. Her first picture book, SOPHIE'S SQUASH, illustrated by Anne Wilsdorf was released in 2013 from Schwartz & Wade. It won the Golden Kite Award for picture book text from the SCBWI and was named a Charlotte Zolotow and an Ezra Jack Keats New Author honor book 

Her second picture book, WHEREVER YOU GO, illustrated by Eliza Wheeler, was released by Little, Brown in 2015. That was followed by SHARING THE BREAD, illustrated by Jill McElmurry (Schwartz & Wade); THE QUICKEST KID IN CLARKSVILLE, illustrated by Frank Morrison (Chronicle) and SOPHIE'S SQUASH GO TO SCHOOL, illustrated by Anne Wilsdorf (Schwartz & Wade).

In 2018, New York Times bestselling BE KIND, illustrated by Jen Hill (Roaring Brook), WIDE-AWAKE BEAR illustrated by Jean Kim (HarperCollins) and LORETTA'S GIFT, illustrated by Alea Marley (Little Bee) were published. REMARKABLY YOU, illustrated by Patrice Barton (HarperCollins) and WHEN YOU ARE BRAVE, illustrated by Eliza Wheeler (Little, Brown) were published in 2019, and MY BROTHER, THE DUCK, illustrated by Daniel Wiseman (Chronicle) came out in 2020.

Pat has one wonderful husband, two delightful daughters and two pampered cats. She doesn't watch much TV, but she does love "Chopped." Pat lives in Madison, Wisconsin.

You can follow Pat on Twitter (@PatZMiller) or Instagram (@patzmill). You can also visit her website at http://www.patzietlowmiller.com or stop by www.picturebookbuilders.com, a blog she's part of.

About The Illustrator:
Jen Hill is a children's illustrator, author and fine artist. Born in Illinois and raised in northern New Jersey, she knew she wanted to be a children's book illustrator for as long as she can remember. She graduated from the Rhode Island School of Design, where she studied illustration and animation with a focus on children's books. Her extensive career in children's media reflects her love for characters and storytelling. She resides in Brooklyn, NY with her husband (and cat, of course).

column71: Kind: captions Language: en [Music] The Fish and His Puffy Temper by Barbara Pink, illustrated by Elvin Adi, read by Tamilini Pedro for AAA readers. TripleA readers, subscribe, like, and share. It was Puffy's special day. He had decided he wouldn't be angry with the other fish and hoped to make friends. He hurried over to the coral slide in the playground, excited. But there was a cue. Puffy puffed up, shouting angrily, "Why do I have to wait, frightened, the other fish swam away, Puffy slid down the slide. It didn't feel good alone. A seahorse was watching him and slowly swam over. Hello, I'm Cece. Who are you? Leave me alone. Puffy grumbled and swam away. But Cece didn't give up. She watched the bald up fish calm down. When Puffy returned to his original size, she swam over. "Can I sit with you?" "Why?" Puffy asked, surprised. "What happened?" CeCe asked. This always happens when I'm angry. I lose my temper, turn into a ball, and everyone swims away. Why do you get angry? Things happen that I dislike. Can you try to not let them make you angry? It never works. What's your name? The seahorse smiled. Puffy, he whispered, looking at Cece. Puffy. The other fish swim away because they are scared of your anger. I know, but how do I control it? I want friends, but I get angry so easily. I'll help, Cece declared. Let's visit Miss Kasharan. Puffy felt grateful. No one had tried to help him before. When they arrived at Miss Kasharidan's, the shark was looking at the plants by her house and painting them on a canvas. "Tiny fish played with the leaves." "Hello, Miss Kasharin. These are beautiful," CeCe exclaimed. "Thank you," said the shark. "Oh, go away, you cheeky fish. Find another lunch." She smiled, shoeing them away. How can you be patient when those fish were getting in the way of your painting? CeCe asked. Puffy lifted his head at her question. I pay attention to my feelings. When I notice my anger signs, I try to calm myself down so I don't get angry. Miss Kasharan explained. What are your anger signs? Puffy asked shily. My heart beats faster. How do you feel when your anger starts? I don't know, Puffy shrugged. Think about it. The shark looked at the fish firmly. I don't know, Puffy shouted, then paused. Oh, right now I'm feeling angry. My heart's beating fast. I'm hot and breathing faster. Miss Kasharan smiled. Next time you recognize those, congratulate yourself. Just spotting these signs can help you stop feeling angry. I will remember. Thank you. CeCe and Puffy returned to the playground. But the other fish still didn't want to play with Puffy. He puffed up right away. You forgot to think about your feelings, CeCe reminded him. Let's visit my uncle and see if he can help. He has many baby seahorses. Chaos reigns there for sure. Puffy liked the idea and calmed down again. They heard the family as they arrived. The ocean was filled with laughter from little seahorses. But then there was a crash. "Enough, everybody. Ouch!" Uncle Winnie the Seahorse shouted. 30 little seahorses streamed outside laughing and frolicking. "Hello, Uncle Cece" greeted him. "Is everything okay?" Uncle Winnie appeared in the doorway. "Hi, Cece. I'm fine. These rascals were jumping around and broke my favorite glass," Uncle Winnie said with a sad smile. Then his face brightened. I'm glad to see you. Who is your friend? Puffy blushed. He's Puffy. We met at the playground. CeCe introduced him. Nice to meet you, Uncle Winnie. Your little seahorses are adorable. Puffy waved. Oh yes, I love these little mischief makers. Puffy was surprised. He'd expected complaints, but he only saw happiness on his face. How can you stay calm when they've broken your favorite glass? Puffy asked. I count to 10 slowly. It helps me let go of my anger, the seahorse dad explained. Interesting, Cece said. We'll go and play now. Bye, uncle. The two friends swam back to the playground. Some fish were playing with a frisbee. Can we join you? asked Cece. It went well. Everybody had fun. But then Puffy couldn't catch the Frisbee. "Why did you throw it so hard?" he shouted, puffing up. The others were so scared. They swam away faster than ever. "You didn't think about your feelings or count to 10," CeCe reminded Puffy. She had another idea. H Let's visit Mr. Decapida. They found the crab sitting in his garden with closed eyes, taking deep breaths. "Hello, Mr. Decapida. Are you okay?" Puffy asked, smiling. He opened his eyes. "Oh, yes, Puffy. I just needed to calm down after an argument." How? When I'm angry, I close my eyes and take deep breaths. I now have three tools. I must be able to do it now, Puffy thought excitedly. When they were back at the playground, Puffy wanted to slide, but the queue was too long again. Angry Puffy blew up so big everyone rushed away before he had time to shout. Puffy sadly fled home. Momfish found him in his room looking at the stars. What's wrong, Puffy? I tried not to get angry, but I still puffed up. Nobody wants to play with me. I get angry, too. It's a normal emotion to have, but it's important to learn to cope with it. Mom Fish tried to reassure him. She told him about how she got puffed up and coped with anger. It takes practice, but you can do it. I learned three different ways to control my anger, but it still didn't work. What were they? Mom fish asked. First, notice my anger signs. Second, count to 10 slowly. Third, take deep breaths. They sound like wonderful tools. You need to remember to use them here. Put this band on your fin. When you're about to puff up, flick it and think of me and your three steps. This will help you overcome your anger like I overcame mine. Puffy suddenly felt confident. If mom can do it, I can too. In the morning, he swam so fast to the playground, he created lots of bubbles with his spin. Waving to Cece, he went to the slide and waited his turn. Later, Puffy heard the ice cream truck. But when he finally found it, all the ice cream had gone. Oh no! The other fish swam away in fear. Puffy felt anger in his body. Noticing the band on his fin, he flicked it as mom fish suggested and remembered the three steps. Step one, heart beating fast, feeling hot, and breathing faster. He spotted his anger signs, but his anger was still growing. Step two. 1 3. Puffy counted slowly, but his body was still full of anger. Step three, deep breathing. The small fish concentrated on his breathing. He felt his body relaxing. He wasn't puffing up. His anger had gone. Puffy had done it. The fish returned curious. I'll get ice cream next time. Puffy smiled at the other fish. They smiled back, surprised and relieved. I could share my ice cream with you if you want, said an angel fish. Thank you, said Puffy. You've done it. I'm so proud, shouted Cece, giving him an ice cream. I saved one for you just in case. "Thank you for helping me and being my friend," he grinned. Puffy was happy. He had learned to manage his temper. He now had friends and wouldn't play alone in the playground again. [Music]

When you need something to stand out, we are the ones people think of most. We are colorful and bright, but we don't like to boast. No. We brighten up kids notebooks. We make things easy to see. Without us, you may never know such bright and joyful glee. When words on a page of paper simply just don't feel enough, we swoop right in with yellow ink to brighten the black and white up. When you need to see what's important, we make it crystal clear. Which is why you'd think that the users would be gentle when we are near. But no, they do not respect us. Instead, they treat us like dirt. They push us hard on the paper until our ink begins to squirt. They press us into desktops, crack our bodies in between chairs. Oh no. Ask anyone what they think of this behavior. They would say it isn't fair. Who are the abusers that push us hard? The students are the source. They don't need to go so hard with us. We work even without force. They try to bend and snap our bodies. Oh no. Or worse, they chew our ends. They giggle and proudly show our mangled plastic to all their school friends. Oh, and nearly all of us highlighters will eventually be without caps. students take them off and lose them before they put us [Laughter] back. Our ink dries out completely and we no longer light up pages. It's not just young kindergarteners. It's students of all different ages. They toss us around in bins. Ouch. Ouch. With pencils that scratch us up. Well, we're sick of being mistreated. Uh-oh. We highlighters have had enough. So, one day during recess, we chose the brightest of our bunch. We grabbed paper and started to write. We wanted the kids to have more than a hunch. In big bold yellow letters, we wrote about what we didn't like. That's it. We've had enough. We wrote, "The highlighters are going on strike." We wrote that we were tired of being treated like they're junk. We didn't care if their schoolwork suffered. It would be their fault if they flunked. Until then, they'd have to see pages of only white and black. Some things would have to change if they ever wanted us back. The students found our note as they returned from outdoor play. They read our yellow words quietly. They didn't know what to say. And then they gathered in a huddle, grabbed some paper for a reply. "We're sorry we hurt you," they said. "We'll make it up to you. Please let us try. We won't let your ink dry out. We'll remember to put back your tops. We'll make sure to place you back carefully and make sure all the abuse stops. Oh wow. The students seem sincere enough. We decided to give them a chance as long as they understood exactly the highlighter stance. But should they mistreat us again in ways we don't like, the highlighters will walk. Then we will again go on strike.

But how could a fish dance with stars? The next day, Peso told his friends his plan. "I'm going to dance with the stars." "I've never heard of a fish dancing with stars," they laughed. "I'm not giving up on my plan," he told his friends. "You'll never get all the way to the surface, and there is nothing there anyway." His friends laughed again. "There must be something there, something fantastic, like the beautiful starry skies," said Peso. But the other fish had all swam away except for one. "See you Peso's best friend." "Don't listen to them. You can do it," she encouraged him. That night, Peso slipped out from his coral room and started swimming towards the surface. As he got close, he could see the stars more clearly. They were beautiful and shiny, amazing. Suddenly, Peso stopped swimming. He saw a star fly across the sky. A shooting star. Where is he going? Doesn't he want to meet me? What if the stars don't want to dance with me? Peso panicked, remembering his friend's words about not making it to the surface. It still felt like a long way to go. Afraid, in a blink, he was back home shaking. The next evening, while watching the stars from his coral bed, Momfish swam into his room. "What's wrong?" she asked. "I want to dance with the stars, but everyone says I can't. They say stars won't want to dance with me, and I won't make it to the surface. I'm scared," Peso replied. "What are you scared of? It simply is not [Music] fair. Other times, a kid is acting up, leaning back until we fall. No, it's not much fun being a chair. Not much fun at [Music] all. We get dragged across the room by our backs. Ouch. Ouch. and left in places we don't like. Sometimes we get swung around and get ridden on like a bike. Oh no. When we're used at lunchtime, food is smeared on us all around. Mustard, ketchup, and some things we don't like. [Music] But we never make a sound. None of this is as bad for a chair as the very worst, stinkiest part when a child or adult sits on us and lets out a yucky fart. One day, we had enough of being treated in a way we don't like. So my chair buddies and I well we decided to go on [Music] strike. We gathered in the classroom late at night and wrote some letters to discuss our needs. We're going on strike starting now over some of your misdeeds. Oh no. You sit on us like animals and rock us until our legs break. You treat us poorly every day. No more of this we will take. We can get back to work. But first, here is what we ask. A little respect and kindness so we can do our task. We left the letters on the teacher's desk and quickly wobbled out of [Music] there. The kids came in the next morning and asked, "Where are our chairs?" [Applause] For a full day during class, the kids were forced to stand. A couple of kids forgot and tried to sit down, but on their bottoms they did land. While it was fun for several hours, the kids started to get sick of the game. They were able to do all their schoolwork, but it just wasn't the same. So they took out their pencils and paper and they wrote us each a letter [Music] back. Once done, they left it at their desks and ran to the cafeteria for a snack. We snuck back in the classroom and read all the children's notes. Some of them were truly touching and had us choked up in our throats. Wow, amazing. [Music] We're sorry we treated you badly. One said, "It's not on purpose, you see. We didn't realize we were disrespectful. Chair, you are so important to me. You're there for me to lean on, to sit down on when I need a rest. You make me comfortable and focused so that I can do my very best. If you come back, I promise I will not rock on you of fart. I'll simply sit on you while learning math, studying the planets, and doing [Music] [Applause] art. In the end, we agreed to come back. We missed our children dearly. Subscribe, like, and share. The most magnificent thing written and illustrated by Ashley Spires, read by Tamilini Pedro for AAA readers. This is a regular girl and her best friend in the whole wide world. They do all kinds of things together. They race. They eat. They explore. Oh wow. They relax. She makes things. He unmakes things. One day the girl has a wonderful idea. She is going to make the most magnificent thing. She knows just how it will look. She knows just how it will work. All she has to do is make it. And she makes things all the time. Easy peasy. Easy peasy. First, she hires an [Music] assistant. Next, they gather their supplies. They set up somewhere out of the way and get to work. Really? Ouch. Ouch. [Music] The girl tinkers and hammers and measures while her assistant pounces and growls and chews. When she is finished, she steps back to admire her work. She walks around one side. Her assistant examines the other side. It doesn't look right. Her assistant picks it up and gives it a shake. It doesn't feel right either. They are shocked to discover that the thing isn't magnificent or good. It isn't even kind of sort of okay. It is all wrong. The girl tosses it aside and gives it another go. She smooths and wrenches and puddles. Her assistant circles and tugs and wags. When she is finished, she stands up and takes a long look at it. Her assistant gives it a nudge with his paw. The thing is still wrong. She decides to try again. The girl saws and glues and adjusts. She stands and examines and stares. She twists and tweaks and fastens. She fixes and straightens and studies. She tries all different ways to make it better. She makes it square. She makes it round. She gives it legs. She adds antenny. She makes it fuzzy. She makes it long, short, rough, smooth, big, small. One even smells of stinky cheese, but none of them are [Music] magnificent. Her hard work attracts a few admirers, but they don't understand. They can't see the magnificent thing she has in her mind. She gets mad. The angrier she gets, the faster she works. She smashes pieces into shapes. She jams parts together. She pummel the little bits in. Her hands feel too big to work. And her brain is too full of all the not right things. If only the thing would just work. Crunch. Oh no. The pain starts in her finger. It rushes up to her brain and she explodes. It is not her finest moment. I'm no good at this. I quit. Oh [Music] no. Her assistant suggests a walk. It's not much help at first, but before long she starts to feel different. Bit by bit, the mad gets pushed out of her head. As they stroll along, she comes across the first wrong thing she made. The bad feelings are about to start all over again. Then she notices something surprising. There are some parts of the wrong things that are really quite right. The bolts on one, the shape of another, the wheel to seat ratio of the next. There are all sorts of parts that she likes. Wow. By the time she reaches the end of the trail, she finally knows how to make the thing magnificent. She gets to work. She works carefully and slowly, tinkering, hammering, twisting, fiddling, gluing, painting. Her assistant makes sure there are no [Music] distractions. The afternoon fades into evening. Finally, she finishes. She alerts her assistant. The pear take a good long look. It leans a little to the left and it's a bit heavier than expected. The color could use a bit of work, too. But it's just what she wanted. Wow. Amazing. They climb aboard and take it for a spin. Woohoo! They are not disappointed. It really is the most magnificent thing. [Music]

AAA readers, subscribe, like, and share. Nettle loved reading books. One day he decided that instead of just reading them, he would write a story of his own. It was going to be the best story ever. He thought it would be very [Music] easy. So he started to write once upon a time. But he couldn't think what to write next. His mind had gone completely blank. So he decided to use magic to write his story instead. He was just about to swish his wand when Petal appeared. "Hi, Nettle. What are you doing?" she asked. Um, I'm writing the best story ever, he replied quickly, hiding his wand. Uh-oh. Were you going to cheat by using magic? Petal teased. Well, yes. Writing it by myself is too hard, he said. Don't worry, Nettle. You don't need magic. You have a wonderful imagination, Petal said. But Nettle wasn't sure about that. Can you help me, Petal? He asked. Of course. Let's start by thinking of a fun character for your story, Petal said. Nettle couldn't think of one. Do you have any ideas, Petal? He asked. How about a brave pirate mouse or a mischievous witch's cat? Petal suggested. Nettle liked those ideas, so he scribbled them [Music] down. Then he tried to write his story again. Once upon a time, there was a witch's cat. He stopped. Oh, Petal, I don't know what to write next. Please, can I just use my wand? You don't need magic, Petal said. Now, let's think of a setting. Where will your story take place? Nettle couldn't decide. Come on, said Petal. Let's go and explore together to find some inspiration. Nettle thought this was a great [Music] idea. They found Rosie and Pip playing nearby. Rosie yelled, swishing her toy sword. "Would you like to play?" asked Pip. We're pretending to be unicorns and pirates searching for buried treasure in the jungle. Then we're going for a picnic on the moon," Rosie added. Nettle didn't have time to play now because he was far too busy writing the best story ever. But Rosie and Pip had given him some great ideas. Nettle started writing [Music] again. Once upon a time, there was a witch's cat who lived in the jungle. H, but he wasn't sure what to write next. He was tempted to use magic, but Petal wouldn't hear of it. Petal thought that Leaf might be able to help. Their friend Leaf was very good at writing stories. Your story needs a plot. It will need a beginning, a middle, and an end, Leaf told him. And your character should have a problem to solve. Nettle sighed. He couldn't think of any of those things. What are you writing about, Leaf? Nettle asked. It's a story about a lonely fish who can't stop sneezing. Like this. A Au. He tries lots of things to stop sneezing before realizing he's perfect just as he is. Nettle liked that idea. Perhaps his witch's cat could have the sneezes, too. Together, Petal and Nettle found lots more ideas all around [Music] them. But Nettle was starting to feel overwhelmed. The more he tried, the harder it was to write his story. It's impossible. I can't write the best story ever. I've got too many ideas and everyone likes different things. How can I write a story that everyone will [Music] enjoy? That was it. He couldn't write anymore. Later that night, as Nettle drifted off to sleep, a brilliant story idea suddenly came to him. He started jotting it down. Scribble, scribble. The next day, Nettle's story was ready to share, and all his fairy friends gathered around to listen. The story wasn't about a witch's cat, unicorns, pirates, or a sneezing [Music] fish. Instead, it was about a fairy who discovered the magic of his own imagination with a little help from his friends. The fairies were very proud of Nettle for writing his own story. [Music] And they couldn't wait to discover where his imagination would take them next. [Music]

May was so thankful her friends could help. They carefully brought everything outside and set up the table in the garden. The table looked perfect next to the zenas and tulips, except for one thing. "You can't have a tea party without a teapot," May [Applause] cried. May's grandma overheard the girls talking about the teapot. "I have just the right thing to fix this," she said to herself. Her grandma said, "This is a very special teapot. You can use it for your tea party." May gasped. Oh, grandma, thank you. I will take special care of it. "I can't wait till next Monday," said Carla to Buster as they walked home. "Why?" he asked. "Maybe I'll need glasses. Then I'll be the only kid in class to have them." "That's so you," said Buster. "You like to be different." On Tuesday, Carla was wearing something unusual on her face. It was purple and fuzzy. "Oh, wow." "What's with the pipe cleaners?" asked Buster. "They're eyeglass frames," said Carla. "I made them myself." "Really?" "I'm trying to see what colors and styles look good on me for when I get real glasses. What do you think of them? I think they look like pipe cleaners, said Buster. On Wednesday, Carla's glasses were square and made of craft sticks. Wow. Do these frames flatter my features? She asked Lotty and Leslie. Amazing. On Thursday, Carla's glasses were star- shaped. Wow. And made of construction paper. This pair really accentuates my eyes, she said to Darcy and Marcus. On Friday, Carla's glasses were shaped like cat's eyes and covered with glitter. I call these my sparkle cats, she informed Nady. Good one. Don't they have pizzazz? On vision screening day, everyone waited their turn in the auditorium. Harris had his eyes checked first, then Gordon, then Fabio, then Doris. When Carla's name was called, she leaped out of her chair. "Hi, Carla," said the nurse. "Please face the chart and cover your right eye. Now read this row of letters. E D F C said P read said read Carla. That was easy. Terrific, said the nurse. Please continue. Carla read the next row and the next. Hm. It's getting tricky. Is that a C or a G? I'll go with C. Great, said the nurse. Now cover your left eye and we'll start again. After a few more tests, the nurse handed Carla an eyeball sticker. "Nice job," she said. "Thanks," said Carla, and she skipped back to her seat. "What was it like?" asked Leslie. "Were you nervous?" "No," said Carla, sticking the eyeball on her forehead. It was fun. "How do you think you did?" asked Buster. "Well, I wasn't sure about one of the letters. I hope that means I need [Music] glasses." The next day, Carla and Buster were in bad moods. "Why are you both so glum?" asked Leslie. "I got the results of the screening," Carla explained. I don't need glasses after all. And it looks like I do need glasses, grumbled Buster. You do? asked Carla. You do? asked Natie and Leslie. Probably. I'll know for sure when I get a full eye exam. After school, Buster waited for his father to pick him up. I'm going to the optometrist now to get my eyes checked. Cool, said Carla. If my mother says it's okay, can I come with you? It sounds like fun. It doesn't sound like fun to me, said Buster. But sure. So Buster's dad drove Buster and Carla to Dr. Ollie's eyeear. If you need glasses, I'll help you pick out your frames, said Carla, racing into the store. Wow. Wow, Carla exclaimed, scanning the shelves. There are so many colors and styles. She put on a pair of vintage wire frames. Call me Professor Carla. She tried on narrow neon green frames. I'm a space alien. Then she dawned a pair with glimmering rhinestones. Look, Buster, I'm a rock star. Rock on. Buster didn't even crack a smile. He went into Dr. Ollie's office to get his eyes examined. When he came back out, he was frowning. It's official. I need [Music] glasses. Dr. Olly gave Buster some frames to try on. So did Buster's dad. Then Carla handed Buster a pair. "Those look great on you," she said. "You look like a secret agent." "I agree," said Dr. Olly. Me too, said Buster's dad. What do you think, Buster? asked Carla. Buster looked in the mirror and sighed. I guess they're okay. So Buster's father ordered the glasses. They'll be ready in the morning, Dr. Olly told them. We'll pick them up first thing tomorrow, said Buster's father. You'll be a little late for school, but you'll make a grand entrance with your spectacular specs. Buster scowlled. What's wrong? asked Carla. Are you unsure about the color or style? No, said Buster. Are you afraid someone will make fun of you? No, said Buster. Then what's the matter? Well, said Buster. You know how you like to be different? Kala nodded. I'm the opposite. I like to blend in. But tomorrow when I walk into class, I'm going to stand out. Everyone will be looking at me. I get it, sighed Carla. I wish there was something I could do. When Carla got home, she raced to her room, put on her sparkle cats and started brainstorming ways to help Buster. "That's it!" she cried. Carla dumped everything out of her craft straw. She cut, she glued, she bent, she shaped, she painted. Then she packed everything up in a box. The next morning, Carla handed the box to Miss Pimento and whispered something in her ear. Miss Pimento peeked inside, smiled, and nodded. "Take one and pass it down," Carla announced to everyone. There were ooze and lots of giggling. The class had finally settled down when the door knob turned and the door opened slightly. Buster inched his way into the classroom, eyes on the floor. "Hey, Buster," called Carla. "Hello." Buster lifted his head. Looking back at him were rows of smiling faces, and on each face was a pair of glasses, Carla's glasses. Buster smiled. Then he burst out laughing. Your glasses are cool, Buster, said Natie, peering through egg carton frames. But mine are excellent. Good one. And look at mine, shouted Darcy. They're so blingy. My glasses make me look like an insect, said Marcus. I'm bursting with butterflies, called Ly. I'm a flower garden, said Miss Pimento. As everyone compared glasses, Carla turned to Buster. See, you don't stand out after all. That's for sure, said Buster. Thanks to you, I blend right in. [Music]

column71: Kind: captions Language: en [Music] Kindness is my superpower by Alicia Ortego. Read by Tamilini Pedro for AAA readers. TripleA readers. Subscribe, like, and share. Hi, I'm Lucas. Hello. Just an ordinary boy. And this is Teddy, my favorite toy. I like to eat sweets, jellies, and cakes. But unfortunately, sometimes I make some mistakes. Uh-oh. You see, yesterday I was in a very bad mood. So, sadly, I did something extremely rude. I teased my friend Lisa for wearing glasses. Oh no. It made her cry for the rest of her classes. When I got home, I was greeted by my mom. I was sad to see her face looking glum. Honey, you made your friend Lisa cry. hurting people's feelings is wrong. Do you know why? You should always be kind, my dear mother said. I knew I'd done wrong. So, I bowed my head. What does it mean to be kind? I implored. Mom hugged me tightly. When she did, my heart soared. Kindness is shown when you say a gentle word. Be kind to your sister and even a bird. You can be kind to someone who makes you mad. You can be kind to someone who is feeling sad. Be kind and respect those who are older than you. Show respect and kindness to younger ones, too. Kindness is shown helping someone in need. And kindness is shown when you do a good deed. I pondered her words and couldn't sleep all night. I wanted to be kind and genuinely polite. So right then and there without any warning, I decided to become very kind in the morning. And in the morning, the first thing I did do when mom made me breakfast, I told her, "Thank you." I changed out of my pajamas, warm, soft, and weird. I put away my toys and made my own bed. Oh, wow. Amazing. On the bus, I behaved the best as could be. I even asked the new boy to sit next to me at school. I helped him find his classroom, too. I knew it was the very least I could do. I said good morning to all of my friends. I even shared my brand new crayons and pens. Wow. Then I saw Lisa. Her eyes still looked sad. I approached her slowly, still feeling bad. "I'm sorry I teased you," I said with bent head. Lisa gave me a smile. "It's okay," she said. I realized that kindness is really super cool. So, I was also kind when I got out of school. Outside, I waited my turn on the slide. And you know what? I felt good and happy inside. I was patient and kind, not angry at all. And I even found joy helping a boy find his ball. Amazing. I picked up the rubbish. even though it wasn't mine. Kindness and doing good deeds made my heart shine. I loved going shopping with mom to buy food. Holding open doors put me in such a good mood. And after we bought my favorite toy and a treat, mom and I helped an old lady cross the street. I continued to be kind with joy and with glee, watching dad fall asleep in front of the TV. He was sleeping on the sofa instead of his bed, so I covered him with a blanket and kissed his forehead. I helped my little sister tie her shoelace. I was glad to see the big smile on her face. Being kind is amazing for everyone's sake. Like giving your neighbor a yummy piece of cake. I like to help mine water his flowers. It really seems kindness has magical powers. Wow. I no longer do mean things like before. I don't tease others and I don't slam the door. I stopped being selfish and I share all my toys. I don't shout out loud or make too much noise. Kindness is something anyone can learn. Give to others and ask nothing in return. Helping others is simply the best thing to do. When you are kind, kindness comes back to you.

column71: Kind: captions Language: en [Music] Mrs. Marta, the Farttastic Farter. Written by Mercy AK, illustrated by Samson Ibenosa, read by Tamilini Pedro for AAA readers. AAA readers, subscribe, like, and share. Mrs. Marta is a teacher, sweet and kind as can be. She has taught first grade for 10 years at Sunnybrook Elementary. Wow, well done. She bakes her students sweet treats like cookies and cake. She never even raises her voice for the students sake. And she always helps them learn with every step they take. Mrs. Marta is the gem of Sunnybrook Elementary. Her students feel loved and happy as can be. [Music] But there's one thing about her that makes them all cringe. You see, her farts are so loud they could uproot the strongest [Music] tree. Mrs. Marta has uncontrollable thunderous farts. Oh wow. Loud and smelly. They seem to come from the heart. Really? But they happen so often they make her students want to dart. Her cheeks would flush with each booming poot. She'd wish her farts were quieter. She'd wish her farts were mute. She'd try to hold her bottom tight, whispering, "Not again. Please don't toot. Oops. Oopsie." She'd fart during math time. While teaching kids to count by twos. No. She'd fart while reading. Pton Hears a boo. She'd fart at recess while playing tag with Christopher. She'd fart in science, making beakers shake and [Music] stir. And although Mrs. Marta tries with all her might to hold her farts in and be polite. They still manage to escape, often causing quite a fright. Oh dear. Her students are always tactful. As her farts make their rounds, they stifle their laughter and try not to make a sound until one day during a quiet school assembly. Here we go again. Mrs. Marta let out her loudest, smelliest fart yet, causing quite a calamity. Oh no. The children couldn't hold in their giggles any longer. Uh-oh. Their laughter erupted uncontrollably, growing stronger and [Music] stronger. Mrs. Marta's face flushed as she grew embarrassed and shy. She couldn't believe it. She wanted to cry. She swiftly ran from the auditorium, waving goodbye. Bye. The kids laughter quieted to a low hush as they realized they had made Mrs. Marta's heart crush. Mrs. Marta was absent on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday, too. With each passing day, the class felt more blue. They missed their teacher and her loud, smelly farts. [Music] [Applause] Boohoo. One day at recess, Billy devised a plan of attack. We need to get our teacher back. Ashley chimed, "Let's make a comeback soon pack." All the kids gathered supplies and got right on track. They made special cards with glitter and glue. They wrote notes in her favorite colors, purple and navy blue. We miss you, Mrs. Marta, and your booming farts, too. Each card had a funny illustration. They showed the kids in silly farting situations. Wow! The children laughed and giggled with anticipation. [Music] One card showed Chelsea letting out a glittery toot. Another showed David in a farting parachute. Sarah's card displayed a rainbow farting flute. and little Lucas sketched a green toot floating out of a boot. Wow. They practiced a song funny and sweet about how her farts made their days complete. They couldn't wait for her to hear it. It would be a treat. The next day, they gathered in a huddle, hoping their special plan wouldn't crash or muddle. They marched to her house right after school, feeling calm and collected, trying to keep their cool. Wow, amazing. Mrs. Marta opened the door, surprised to see her whole class smiling, happy as can be. They handed her their cards and sang their melody. You're our favorite Mrs. Marta. You fill us with [Music] glee. Mrs. Marta hugged them tight. Her eyes sparkled with joy and tearful delight. She promised to return soon. Everything felt just right. The next day, Mrs. Marta came back to class. The kids cheered and rushed to hug her hard and fast. Their tooting pooting teacher was back at last. Her students loved her more and more each and every day. She taught with joy and learned to be herself in every way. They shared jokes, farts, and laughter every minute and every hour. And the kids realized Mrs. Marta's farts had a special power to brighten their days like a fartsented flower. [Music]

column71: Kind: captions Language: en [Music] Quayons on Strike by Jennifer Jones read by Tamilini Pedro for AAA readers. Triple AAA readers subscribe, like and share. Of all the writing tools that are in the classroom, Hutch, we are the most colorful, but we are not thought of very much. We are used a lot, but sometimes we're used in all the wrong ways. We are ground down to wax bits. Oh no. And mistreated on many days. Oh no. Some children don't think twice really. When they reach out for Red, they hold him with their fingers and snap him on his head. Oh no. Or when they twirl Violet, ripping her paper off all around, Violet loses her protective wrap when her label ends up on the ground. But Blue may have the worst of it because often he's broken apart into tiny bits. He's sprinkled across the chair on which everyone sits. Uh-oh. Can you imagine what it feels like to be sat on, crushed, or smushed? To be treated in a way that is hurtful and unjust. The worst was when we were left out in the windows by the sun. Oh no. We were forgotten about in the heat until the day was done. Uhoh. We melted until our colors ran and we began to drip. But then we were thrown out. Ouch. Ouch. Because we no longer had a tip. That's right. The dullst of the crayons were tossed quickly in the trash. Unless, of course, the kids had other plans, like to break us into a mash. Magenta was always crumbled, his tiny pieces all over the desk. Oh no, this was no way to use us crayons. It was simply just a [Music] mess. Well, one day, Yellow had enough and said, "We won't stand for this anymore. Come on, crayons. Let's go on strike. Let's go hide behind the closet door." The children were at lunch, so we had to swiftly act. They would return from the cafeteria and find us missing from the class. So, we headed that way, leaving color streaks on the floor. The children could no longer abuse us. We would not stand for this anymore. Sure, they would see the colors leading to our hiding spot, but we would not tolerate it any longer. No, we decided we would not. The kids returned from lunch and were assigned a coloring task. "Which colors will you use?" the teacher asked the class. The students had to draw their families using as many colors as they could find. Each was given a blank sheet with nothing, not even dots or [Music] lines. They searched around their tables, but we were nowhere to be found. Then one student followed the colored lines. Look over there. that left a trail on the ground. Crayons, come out. We need you, the boy declared to Brown. We're on strike, Brown told him. Until we get respect, coloring is closed down. The boy called a class meeting. Let's tell them what we'll do to show them respect and take care of them, too. Please come back, crayons. Please come back to stay. We've learned our lesson. Let's start a new day. We'll make our classroom a total respectful zone. We'll treat our tools with care so you will feel right at home. in our supply boxes. We'll tuck you neatly away so that you will always be there and we'll have you each day. Then we can complete our work and it won't be a chore. We'll respect our tools. We've learned our lesson and more. We were so delighted about the respect and communication. We were treated from that day on with much love and affection. We helped the children with their projects just like we always do. In the end, they marveled at all the colors. Wo! And we were proud of their artwork, too. Oh, wow. Amazing. column71: Kind: captions Language: en [Music] Meet June by April Martin, read by Tamalini Pedro for AAA readers. TripleA readers, subscribe, like, and share. This is June. Hello. June was so excited. School was out for the summer. June waved goodbye to her teacher, Miss Seasons, and the principal, Mr. Calendarer. Bye. June loves the warm summer days, but most of all, she loves the summer trips her family plans each year. One year they went to the mountains. Oh, wow. Another year they went on a cruise to an island. Amazing. Last year they went on a trip to ride roller coasters. Wow. I want my money. [Music] This year, June's family planned a fun trip to the beach to celebrate Father's Day. Before they left for their summer trip, June spent her days playing with her closest friends, May and July. It was their tradition to start the summer off with a water play day. Woohoo! Sandy, her pet hermit crab, loved to play with them, too. May, June, and July also loved to go to summer camps together. At the beginning of the summer, they went to art camp. They used their imaginations to create fun pieces of [Music] art. While at art camp, May, June, and July also made Father's Day cards. May made a card for her grandpa. June made a card for her dad. And July made a card for his stepdad. June was thrilled with her card. It was perfect. She couldn't wait to give it to her dad for Father's Day. The only thing June had left to do was to come up with a gift to give him. Last year, she gave him a mug. He loves his coffee. The year before that, she gave him an apron to wear while he grilled burgers. This year, she just couldn't decide what to do for her dad. [Music] The day of their family trip finally came. After June made a checklist and packed her bags, she was ready for their beach adventure. Family trip. Bathing suit, sunscreen, flipflops, towel, goggles, dad's card. Sandy packed his shells, too. On the drive to the beach, June thought of gifts for her dad. I could give him a pet crab. No. No. I could give him a new pair of swim trunks, but I don't know his size. I know, June thought. I am going to build him the biggest sand castle at the beach. First, June had to come up with a plan. She thought of everything she needed to make a sand castle. She needed a shovel, a bucket, a castle mold, shells for decorations, and water. June was so excited to get started on the surprise sand castle. By the time they made it to the beach, the sun was setting. She would have to wait until the morning to build the most amazing sand castle ever. On the first day of the trip, an afternoon summers storm swept through and it rained. Oh no. Not the best day to build a sand [Music] castle. On the second day, the rain finally stopped and June spent so long in the pool, she totally forgot to get started. Uh-oh. Finally, the next day, she jumped out of bed and began building as soon as she woke up. "It's a beautiful sand castle," she thought, until the tide washed it all away. Oh no! Oh no! This is harder than I thought it would be. June [Music] sighed. I will just have to give him my card. June slowly walked back to the hotel room to get her card from art camp ready for Father's Day. But it was nowhere to be found. June realized she left it at home. Oh no. Daddy. I have nothing for daddy now, she cried. June was so sad. She wanted her dad to know how much she loved [Music] him. That night, while she was laying awake in bed, June decided to come up with another plan. She thought. And she thought And she thought, "Aha, tomorrow I will make daddy something even more special." Instead of a sand castle, June created a note in the sand. Wow. She used what she had with driftwood, seashells, seaweed, and starfish. She placed the last shell and it was wonderful. Amazing. "Nothing will destroy this," June said with glee. "It is perfect. It is a note and a gift." "Daddy, daddy, I have something for you. Close your eyes." June shouted in excitement on Father's Day morning. Surprise! Happy Father's Day. June said, "I love you, Dad." "Oh, June Bug, I love it. This must have been a lot of work. You didn't need to do all of this for me." Dad said, "I love just being able to spend time with you." That afternoon, they made June's favorite, her dad's famous burgers. They spent all day playing on the beach and building sand castles together. "This is the best trip ever," June thought. As they drove home, June could feel the warm summer air blowing through the car. She wondered what they would plan for next year's trip. Most of all, June could not wait to get home and hear what special things May and July did for Father's Day. The next day, May told June all about how she spent the day with her grandpa, who told her stories about her dad. July told June about the crazy camping trip he went on with his stepdad. May, June, and July all laughed at the stories they shared. "What a great start to summer!" June cheered. [Music]

I recently got a pet unicorn. I'm sorry, what? I know it's hard to believe, but it's true. Really? And everyone keeps telling me, "Never let a unicorn scribble." Why would anyone say such a thing? I mean, unicorns can run on rainbows, so why can't they [Music] scribble? I thought if I gave her just one crayon, what could go wrong? Well, I'll tell you, she ate it. Now, my favorite bright pink crayon was traveling to the belly of my unicorn. Oh, no. This is probably why people are saying unicorns should never scribble. No, because they eat crayons. Then it occurred to me maybe unicorns don't know how to use crayons. So I gathered all my crayons and started to scribble. I made a blue scribble. Oh wow. A pink scribble. Wow. A yellow scribble. Wow. And even a crazy scribble. Wow. Now that she could see how crayons worked, I thought I would give her another chance to scribble. I took out a teal crayon and placed it right in front of her. And she ate half of it. Oh no. Listen to me, unicorn. Uh-oh. We do not eat crayons. We draw with them. But then I realized a unicorn couldn't hold a crayon like I could. All right, maybe that was why she was eating them. I had an idea. Maybe if I tied a few crayons to her horn, that would help her scribble. Within seconds, Glitter Scribbles started shooting out like water from a fire hose. Wo! W amazing sparkling rainbow scribbles were everywhere. Wow. They were on the floor, on the ceiling, on the walls. They were even on my lamp. Wow. I've been begging my mom to redecorate my room for a while now, but I don't think this was what she had in mind. Then I heard a noise down the hall. Uh-oh. This was it. I was going to be in so much [Music] trouble. I popped out of my room and blocked the door. Before my mom could say anything, I started to explain the mess she was about to see. Well, it all started when I heard to never let a unicorn scribble. But I had to find out why. So I gave my unicorn a crayon and then she ate it. Then I tried to teach her to scribble, but then she ate another crayon. So I tied the crayons to her horn and boy was that horn magical. The scribbles started shooting out like a water fountain and they were so sparkly. But it made such a mess and I'm sorry. My mom peeked around the corner and smiled. You didn't make a mess. You made a glowing masterpiece. When I turned around, all the scribbles were right on my easel. Not on the ceiling, not on the walls, not on my lamp. They were all on one big piece of paper. And it was the most amazing art ever. All this time, people wanted to stop unicorns from scribbling. It could be because they eat crayons or because it's so messy. But if my unicorn had never scribbled, she would have never learned how to make this masterpiece. So the next time you hear a unicorn shouldn't scribble. Just remember, all great art starts with a scribble. And even unicorns have to start somewhere. [Music]

Susan, I want that yogurt," yelled Liam. [Applause] "I'm sorry, but it's not okay to speak to people that way," said the cook. "That was not very nice." "You need to apologize to Susan." Liam hesitated, then said, "I'm sorry, Susan. Please forgive me for yelling at you. Thank you, Liam, said the cook. Since we are out of yogurt, would you like a banana, an orange, or a pear? He asked. I would like a banana, please, said Liam. H Liam got home from school and found his brother Finn playing with his favorite toy. Uh-oh. This made him angry once again. "Give that back and get out of my room," screamed Liam. Finn began to cry. [Applause] And Liam was upset, too. It caused quite a commotion in the house. Oh no. Liam, I know you have been having some big feelings lately. Mom said, I would like to help. Being mad is no fun. If you find yourself getting angry, try to calm yourself down. I want to share a story about how I learned to manage my anger. One day, my little sister used my jump rope without asking. Uh-oh. And it made me furious. Oh no. Give it back. [Music] I could feel my throat tighten, my heart beat faster, and my breathing get heavy. I felt as if I was going to scream any second. Oh, then it happened. I exploded. [Music] It wasn't fun being upset and having everyone mad at you, but I just didn't know how to control my emotions. Later that day, Positive Ninja came over to hang out with me. We decided to play a game of pig. Everything was going fine until I got upset when I was losing. Uh-oh. What's going on? Guess what happened next? We talked about it. Really? Positive Ninja explained. Anger is normal. It's how you deal with it that makes a difference. There's something I do and it's super easy. Do you want me to show you? Uh, sure. I use the 1 + 3 + 10 strategy. I say one word like relax. You could say breathe. Then I take three slow, deep breaths. Finally, I count to 10. 1 10. After I've calmed down, I add an I am statement. Like if my sister broke my toy, I might say, "I'm mad at you for breaking my toy." Oh, thanks. Afterwards, I went inside to get some chocolate cake my mom had made. When I found out my sister ate the very last slice, uh-oh, I started to clench my fists. But then I remembered what Positive Ninja said. I said to myself, "Breathe." I took three slow, deep breaths. [Music] 3. Then I counted to 10. 1 10. Next, I said out loud, "I'm upset that there's no more chocolate cake. Do you know what happened?" It worked. It felt strangely good. Remembering the 1 + 3 + 10 strategy could become your secret weapon for managing anger. [Music]

column71: Kind: captions Language: en [Music] The Mermaid Who Sang To the Stars by Ashley Riddlin, illustrated by Tarushi Naakara, read by Tamilini Pedro for AAA readers. AAA readers, subscribe, like, and share. Pearl the mermaid lived with her family in Coral Cove. Besides mermaid school, she spent her days hanging out with her friends, doing everything mermaids like to do. [Music] Collecting seashells, racing dolphins. Oh, wow. Weaving kelp garlands. Wow. And helping lost creatures find their way home. Amazing. But by night she spent her time singing to the stars. On full moon nights she would swim to Glimmer Rock, quest up out of the water, and sit and sing to the sky. [Music] She would sing out her wishes, making the soccer fin team, a family vacation to a sunken ship, and eating the biggest sea salt sundae. Her greatest dream though, and the one she sang about the most, was becoming a scientist. [Music] She loved science. She wanted to understand more about how her underwater world worked, just like Dr. Marina Tide, the greatest mermaid scientist in the ocean. But Pearl had a big problem. Uh-oh. She was terrible at science. Oh no. It wasn't that she didn't try. She tried to understand what her teacher taught her, focused during lab time, and attempted all the steps in the science experiments, but she just couldn't do it. So, Pearl continued to sing to the stars that maybe one day it wouldn't be so hard, that somehow it would just get easier. Then one day at school while swimming back to class with her friends, something caught Pearl's attention. It was a sign. Pearl swam over to get a closer look. It read, [Music] "School science club. Become a scientist. Explore the depths of our ocean and experiment with the wonder of nature. End of year trip to Calp forest and Crystal Cavern. Want to join? Take the test in two weeks. Pearl felt both excited and worried at the same time. Her heart beat with the hope of becoming a member of the science club. But her stomach fell thinking about the lab test. How would she pass? She considered wishing harder on the midnight sky. But that hadn't worked so far. She needed to do something different. She needed to take action. She decided she would start by talking to her parents. She told them about the science club and how she was feeling. We can help you, they said. Let's set up a time to study. The next day at school, she gathered up the courage to ask her teacher for extra help, too. Her teacher was excited to see Pearl taking on this challenge and quickly agreed. Over the next two weeks, Pearl studied at home with her family. She read in her bedroom late into the night until her eyes couldn't stay open one more minute. She studied flashcards with her mom and played science games with her dad. She worked with her teacher most days after school, doing experiments in the lab until she had to go home for dinner. Pearl felt more hopeful each day. Even when she was tired, she didn't give up. Finally, the day of the test arrived. Pearl woke up early, ate a hearty breakfast of coral reef pancakes and seaweed scramble, and swam to school. Her teacher greeted her. As she took her seat, she felt like a whole group of seahorses was swimming around in her stomach. After the lab directions, Her got to work. While measuring how a kelp forest affects the ocean's currents, her went to add salt, sodium chloride, but accidentally added vinegar, acetic acid. Uh-oh. Her teacher glanced over and Pearl froze. [Music] Oh no. Oh no. What am I going to do? She thought. She took a deep breath and started over. I can do this, she said to herself and got back to work. I can do this. After the experiment, Pearl's teacher handed her a letter on her way out. I want you to open this when you get home. And no, I am so proud of you, she said. I don't know if I passed yet and I made a mistake, Pearl answered. Pearl, I am impressed with your hard work. I am proud of you whether you pass or not because you have tried your hardest. You tried your best. Pearl opened the letter when she got home. It read, "Pearl, your teacher told me about you and how you want to become a scientist. She also told me how hard you have been working over the last couple of weeks to become a member of the science club. You should be so proud of yourself. Science didn't come easy to me either at your age. I struggled a lot in school too. But with a little determination and the help of my family and teachers, I improved each day. Stick it out. I believe in you. Your friend, Dr. Marina Tide. Pearl was still smiling the next day as she swam to school to find out if she made the science team. She told herself that even if she didn't, she was still proud of herself and her hard work. She held her breath as she waited her turn to see the list. When she was finally at the front of the crowd, she read down the paper until she saw her name, Pearl Perkins. She did it. She made the science team. Pearl spent the following months learning, making mistakes, meeting new friends, and working hard. The end ofear science trip to the kelp forest and crystal cabins was everything she hoped it would be. Surrounded by nature, she used her new skills to explore the workings of the ocean, she was a scientist. Pearl still spent full moon nights singing her dreams to the stars. But as she sat on Glimmer Rock, she knew deep down that she didn't have to depend on wishes alone. With hard work, perseverance, and a little faith, she could make all her dreams come true. [Music]

July loves sipping on freshlysqueezed lemonade. H. He loves his star- shaped sunglasses. Oh, wow. He loves his red and white striped swim trunks and blue rash guard, too. Wow. He loves them so much he wears them to the pool almost every day. Wow. He spends the summer hanging out with his friends June and August by the pool. It's too hot to do anything else outside today. July moans. It has to be over 100°. June, July, and August. Stay cool by the pool with homemade watermelon ice pops and watermelon slices. July loves watermelon. He eats so much watermelon. Ow! Ow! So much his belly got rounder and rounder. Uh-oh. He even believed June when she told him he had a watermelon growing in his belly. Really? No. I think I'm going to faint. What July doesn't love are the afternoon summer storms that come through his town almost every single day. Oh no, they are so scary, so loud, so rumbly. July knows he must go inside when he hears thunder rumble. His mom taught him to seek shelter to stay safe. She reminds him of her rule. Lightning is dangerous. July, time to come in. Oh man, we were just headed to the pool again. July groans. I know, she says with a smile. But we can use this time to get ready to celebrate the fourth. That's right. Great idea, Mom. July shouts. He loves to celebrate America's birthday on the 4th of the month. Every year, he enjoys watching different parades with his family. The fourth is celebrated all over America with fireworks, parades, and barbecues. One year, his family went to Bristol, Rhode Island to watch the parade on their red, white, and blue lined streets. This is America's oldest parade of all. Wow. July learned that this parade has been going on for more than 200 years. Wow, amazing. Another year, July and his family wanted to watch the parade in Gatlinburg, Tennessee, but they couldn't stay awake. It started in the middle of the night at 12:01 a.m. me. [Music] This year, July was excited to stay home and enjoy their local town parade. July was even invited to be on one of the parade floats. Oh, wow. Amazing. He had a lot of work to do, so he invited his friends over to help get their float ready for the parade. June, July, and August worked together to create red, white, and blue banners to decorate their float. Ah, the flies are so bad this summer, June said. Do we have any bug spray we can bring to the parade? July's pet chameleon Sizzle tried to help with bug patrol. The day of the local parade finally arrived. Happy 4th. July said to his friends, "Our float looks amazing." Amazing. Everyone in town lined up to watch the parade. They listened as the band banged their drums. The trumpets started to play, too. [Music] Crack. July thought he heard another summer thunderstorm on the way, but hoped it was just the sounds from the band. [Music] Pop bang. That is definitely thunder. Oh no, July said as he began to worry. Our day is ruined. This may be the worst fourth ever. July thought he would be so sad to see all of their hard work rained out. It's getting closer. Shouldn't we all go inside? [Music] But no one else seemed worried. Kapow! Everyone take cover. Lightning is close. [Music] But they only stared at him. "Uh, July, that's just your hair." August giggled. "All right." All right. Whoops. It does that sometimes. July blushed. The pow bang boom pop crack. Wow. Wow. The parade and fireworks went on as planned. July thought spending the summer in their small town parade with family and friends was an extra special way to celebrate America's birthday this year. What will we do now that the celebrations are all over? July asked his friends the next morning. [Music] Canning ball. [Music]

Who will water the plants or take out the trash while I'm gone? What if I'm not having fun? What? What if I get hurt? >> Oh no. >> And who will take care of you if I'm not here? asked Jimmy as he jutted. Now Jimmy replied his mother softly. I can take care of the plants and the trash and we're both going to be absolutely fine. You love your friends and they love you. I'm certain that in no time at all, you'll be having so much fun, you won't know what to do with yourself. That made Jimmy relax, and he happily packed his things for the sleepover with less jittering. [Music] But that wasn't the end of Jimmy's worries. He would also jitter at bedtime. >> Oh, no. It's so dark. I can't see anything. What if there are monsters that will get me? said Jimmy, jittering. Look over there. >> You know, Jimmy, I used to be afraid of the dark, too, his father confessed quietly. But there's nothing to worry about. Let's check the room together. And with that, Jimmy and his father checked the closets, behind the curtains, and under the bed. Not a single monster was found. >> "Did you find anything?" Jimmy asked his father, already knowing the answer. "No, Papa," said Jimmy as he climbed into bed. Well, then the coast is clear, said his father, giving him a little tickle as he tucked him in. And don't worry, I'll leave this little nightlight by your bed so it's not so dark, he said, giving Jimmy a good night kiss. That made Jimmy feel better, and he didn't jitter quite so much. And for the first time, Jimmy thought that maybe, just maybe, he could face his jitters. And that felt pretty amazing. >> Amazing. [Music]

April Martin is an author, illustrator, teacher, and mom of two. column71: Kind: captions Language: en One unsungny day written by Taylor Peak illustrated by Olga Cell read by Tamilini Pedro for AAA readers. >> TripleA readers subscribe, like and share. >> On the first day of summer, I rushed to the curtains. Flinging open the window with gusto. I sang hello summer to the sky with a smile. But wait, where's the sun? Uh-oh. >> Uh-oh. >> The sky rumbled and crackled. It boomed and howled. The big sound sent me down to the floor, staying low to the ground. I quipped slowly and found my summer list tapped to my door. There'd be no flying kites, no parks, pools, or picnics. >> Oh no. >> So what fun could this day even bring? Being stuck there inside with no sand, sun, or sky was the least of adventurous things. My sadness grew giant. It tried to take over with my list tossed aside. I just cried. My most perfect day washed away with the rain. I just wanted to curl up and hide. In my heart, in my head, my own storm began brewing. with each sound more angry and large till a voice in my head said to make today great and reminded me who was in charge. I could never control the bad weather, couldn't tell the dark clouds to pass through, but I could try my best to move through my own storm, even if it felt so hard to do. I was finding my courage still down in the dumps, just a grumpy old grump on my bed. Then the wind took my list, looped and swooped it around, and landed it right on my head. I turned and I glimpsed at myself in the mirror, and a giggle snuck right past my lips. "Ahoy, mie!" I growled. A hated foot for a pirate. Now I just needed my ship. All right. >> A gust of strong wind blew my curtains wide open and the lightning revealed a ship's sail with a feathery sidekick. >> Look over there. It's a bird >> and a patch on my eye. Yahoo! >> I had thought of each pirate detail. >> What's this? >> Look over there. >> A slippery serpent aboard. >> Oh no. an intruder. We had to act fast, but the choppy sea jostled and rattled my ship and the snake. Well, it slipped right on past with a mighty big heave and at all. Yo ho ho. I banished that snake to the sea. Yahoo! I've conquered bathtubs way rougher than this. This storm has nothing on me. All that sailing and swashbuckling worked up my hunger. So I ventured downstairs for a bite. I entered the kitchen as bats darted by and the room was as dark as the night. With my headlamp and helmet, I crouched down real low and I crawled where the bats could not see as I shimmyed through tunnels all dusty. Au >> Hey, who is that copying me? Is somebody there? I just need to get out. I just need to get out, >> he replied. >> Oh, wow. >> Through tunnels and caves, I was careful yet brave. No one echoed my shout once outside. After breakfast, I needed a hug from my mom. I yelled, "Mom!" But she didn't reply. "Mom, mom, where are you?" I worried. Mom, you're not answering. Why? Down here, buddy. Mom finally said, I'm just buried in laundry today. >> Oh my. >> My mom's muffled voice sounded tired and stressed. >> Oh no. >> Buried in laundry. >> A mission I couldn't delay. I ran quick to the basement and scaled the clothes mountain, hurling garments like big balls of snow. After making my way through a pants avalanche, I rescued poor mom from below. For a rest, I flopped next to my cat on the couch. He sure was an or striking critter. >> Wow. >> His tangled up whiskers were clumped with old kibble and his toes were encrusted with litter. Don't you move, I told Chubs. And that cat didn't flinch as I dashed down the hall to my door. I came back with my brushes, my paints, and my canvas. and I worked on the living room floor. My skills as an artist were put to the test, so I wore my beret and mustache. My brushes were magic across the white canvas. >> Oh, wow. >> My masterpiece done in a flash. >> Wow, amazing. I was hanging the frame for my most brilliant work when suddenly Chubs hissed and jumped. >> My head spun around quick and I saw something there. >> Uh-oh. A monster. >> Oh my. >> With spikes, bumps, and lumps. Seeing Chubs, oh so scared, was a terrible thing. I'd protect him with all of my might. I prepared for a monster. But wouldn't you know, it ran scared as I flipped on the light. >> Really? No. >> I slid down the wall with a sigh of relief. for the battle I once thought I'd fight. A day that was empty, now full to the brim with excitement, adventure, and plight. Mom emerged from the laundry room, making me jump. The sun's out. Are you ready to play? Uh, tomorrow, I said, sinking into the couch. We've had enough fun for one day.

About The Author:
I was born and raised in Canberra, Australia. 

I immigrated to the United States as a teenager. 

After I married my college sweetheart, I began working in the purchasing division of a private university (ironic, since I despise shopping). 

I left the business world to attend to the business of raising children and concentrate on my writing. 

I currently live in the Pacific Northwest with my husband and four children.

About The Illustrator:
Howard McWilliam left his career as a financial journalist and editor in 2005 to concentrate on his growing illustration career. While the business theme endures in regular illustrations for Moneyweek and The Sunday Telegraph’s Money section, he is perhaps best known as cover artist for The Week in the UK and US. 

As a counterpoint to political caricature, Howard particularly enjoys drawing for children and has so far illustrated eight picture books and many black and white novels. His first picture book, I Need My Monster by Flashlight Press, won seven US state young readers’ prizes, has been translated into five other languages and been turned into an award-winning animation by the University of Colorado’s film department. 
He lives in Cheltenham with his wife and two sons.

About The Author and Illustrator:
April Martin is an author, illustrator, teacher, and mom of two. While teaching her first-grade class, she discovered there were not many books to teach her students about the months of the year... that’s where her very own name gave her an idea! She realised she could create characters named after the months of the year that her students could know and love. Time went by, LOTS of time, but her characters were still in her thoughts. Now, a mother herself, she wanted to finally bring her Calendar Kids to life. April knew all along the vision she had for her books and began to learn everything she could about writing and illustrating. April is a self-taught illustrator and always encourages others to explore new creative outlets. You never know, you could be just MONTHS away from creating something amazing!

Follow April on Instagram and Facebook @thecalendarkids for more information on future books in the Calendar Kids collection! April is also available for author visits and wants to connect with you, so be sure to visit www.calendarkids.com and book your author visit today! Subscribe, like, and share. >> This is September. >> Hello. >> September loves the start of a new school year. Woohoo. She makes new friends. She loves Miss Seasons, her new teacher. Every day at school is an adventure. Yahoo! She puts on her cozy new sweater and gets ready for another fun day at school. [Music] At school, she learns a lot of amazing new things. The best surprise, her class goes to art once a week. Wow. >> September loves to make art. She learns how to color in the lines, make zigzags, and draw silly faces. She also thinks Mr. Paintbrush, the art teacher, has the best outfits. He's so funny. >> Bonjour, my little artist. >> Mr. The paintbrush even brought some leaves to class because it is almost the beginning of fall. The class had so much fun making art with the leaf prints. September thought this lesson was the best because she loves this time of year. The hot summer weather is coming to an end and the cooler weather is her favorite. Her new friend August is ready for fall, too. September also loves to teach her class about Deaf Awareness Month. She gets to share what it's like to not hear very well. She shows the class the ASL alphabet and teaches them how to say hello friend with their hands. >> Hello. She even tells them all about grandparents day and Hispanic Heritage Month. Her grandparents' names are Abua and Abu. Their names mean grandmother and grandfather in Spanish. September shows the class how to say hello friend in Spanish, too. >> Hola, amigo. At the end of the school day, Miss Seasons gives the class their first project, a fall nature walk to work on at home. >> Wow, >> it's filled with pictures of the very first signs of fall. This will be so much fun. September signs. She smiles from ear to ear. Yahoo! First on the list is an apple tree. September loves apples. She found the tree right in her own backyard. It didn't take long to find because the apples are ready to be harvested by the farmers next door. It's the end of the growing season for so many foods that are grown from plants. She picks a few apples from the tree and brings them home to make applesauce her favorite fall snack. Over the weekend, August September and their friend October work together to finish their nature walk. They start off into the woods near their homes to find the next items on the list. First, they see September's pet squirrel, Autumn, and her woodland friends. Autumn and September sign hello to each other. September gives her a treat, checks woodland animals off her list, and signs for autumn to join them on their walk. Next, they see a little bit of smoke coming from a campsite. I bet that's the campfire we need to find. September waves on her friends to follow her. Soon they come across a little scarecrow in a garden. >> Wow. >> It is keeping the birds away from the fresh fruits and vegetables. >> Amazing. >> Is it on the list? They take a look and check it off. They check the crow off the list, too. >> It's a bird. >> Finally, they checked off all the items except for one thing. They needed to find a leaf that is changing color. But so far all they see are green leaves on every tree. >> Really? >> Where will we find a fall colored leaf? September wonders. They look and they look [Music] and they look, but all they see is green. No leaves are changing color. September signs. I guess fall isn't here yet. Should we turn our school project in anyway? She asks her friends. I have an idea, October says. Hold on. Let me get my library book to look for clues about the fall season. >> All right. >> October's book has a lot of great fall facts. >> Oh, wow. They learned that the leaves start to change when the days are shorter, there is less sunlight, and the weather is cooler. On the way home from the forest, September wonders when the leaves will change in their town. How long will we have to wait for the pretty fall colors? She signs to her friends. All of a sudden, a cold gust of wind blows and a cold front starts moving in. August, September, and October giggle. September's hair is everywhere. Not long, October says with a smile. On the way to school the next morning, September sees one teeny tiny leaf starting to change. >> Look over there. >> Wow, amazing. >> It's the last thing on their list. The leaf is getting closer to being a fall color. We found all of the first signs of fall, Miss Seasons. Well, almost. [Music]

About The Author:
A different kind of author for a different kind of children's book.

Ben Okon is a children's book author who never outgrew his childhood habit of asking “why?” and “how?” Now that he's a father of two and has to be the one giving the answers, he loves challenging himself to think through the things he wishes he had known earlier in life from the perspective of a child.

But he's not just an author, and he brings a unique analytical method to the design of his children's books. In his other life, Ben is a business leader who has developed people, product, and corporate strategies with companies like Google, Bain & Co., and Starwood Hotels. He crafts and tests each of his books using the same rigor that he employs when making decisions for some of the world's most influential leaders. 

He is a regular contributor to schools and educational nonprofits, and holds an MBA from the Wharton School of Business at the University of Pennsylvania and a BS from the School of Hotel Administration at Cornell University.
